lead: Saturday closes the week with two lessons in humility before God. Hebrews asks Christians to accept hardship as a father's training and to pursue peace and holiness. In Luke two men pray in the temple, and only one goes home justified. Both readings ask who will see the Lord: the one who lets God correct him, and the one who asks for mercy.

r.h: The Lord disciplines those whom he loves
set: The readers have suffered, but “not yet” to the point of blood (v. 4). The writer helps them to understand their hardships by quoting Proverbs 3:11–12. In the ancient world it was taken for granted that a good father trains his children, with teaching and correction together. The writer does not say that every suffering is a punishment for a particular sin (compare John 9:3). He says that God can use every hardship to form his children.
str: vv. 7–11: discipline as a father's training, and its peaceful fruit.
vv. 12–13: strengthen weak knees, make straight paths.
vv. 14–17: pursue peace and holiness; the warning of Esau.
kw: The whole upbringing of a child: teaching, training and correction. The word comes from pais, child.
Being made holy, set apart for God. Verse 10 says that God trains us so “that we may share his holiness”.
Profane, the opposite of holy: one who treats sacred things as common. Esau treated his birthright, the gift of God's promise, as worth one meal.
vv: for the Lord disciplines those whom he loves,
Proverbs 3:12. The discipline is the proof of the love, not its opposite.
Now, discipline always seems painful rather than pleasant at the time, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
“Trained” is an athletic word, gegymnasmenois, from which “gymnasium” comes. The fruit comes “later”.
See to it that no one becomes like Esau, an immoral and godless person, who sold his birthright for a single meal.
Genesis 25:29–34. Esau traded a lasting gift for a passing hunger. Verse 17 recalls his tears when the blessing went to Jacob (Genesis 27:34–38).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross: there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle, and spiritual progress involves discipline and self-denial that lead gradually to the peace and joy of the Beatitudes (CCC 2015). Verse 14, holiness “without which no one will see the Lord”, echoes the Beatitude of the pure in heart, who will see God (Matthew 5:8).

r.h: God, be merciful to me, a sinner
set: Luke says plainly to whom the parable is told: “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt” (18:9). Two men go up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee's practices go beyond what the Law required: the Law commanded fasting on the Day of Atonement, and he fasts twice a week; he tithes all he receives. What he says about himself is true. The trouble is the comparison and the contempt. The parable does not portray all Pharisees; it portrays a temptation that every devout person, Christians first of all, can fall into.
str: v. 9: to whom the parable is told.
v. 14: the verdict, and the saying about exalting and humbling.
kw: Treating others as nothing. This, more than his fasting, is what Jesus exposes.
A plea for atonement. The word is related to hilastērion, the mercy seat over the ark (Hebrews 9:5). He asks God to cover his sin.
Made right with God. It is God's verdict, not the man's own claim.
vv: God, I thank you that I am not like other people:
The prayer begins with thanks, but it is really about himself. He asks for nothing, and so receives nothing.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner!
He stands far off, does not look up, and beats his breast. His prayer is short and true. The Greek says “the sinner”, as if there were no other.
for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but all who humble themselves will be exalted.
The same saying closes the parable of the places at table (14:11). In both, God is the one who lifts up.
ch: The Catechism calls humility the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559), and names this parable as the third of Luke's parables on prayer, the prayer of the humble heart (CCC 2613). The cry of the tax collector, joined with that of the blind men, lives on in the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern Churches, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners” (CCC 2667). In our Holy Qurbono the people answer again and again, “Kurielaison”, Lord, have mercy: the prayer of the tax collector on the lips of the whole Church.

qa: What does Hebrews mean when it says Esau “found no chance to repent”?

Genesis tells that Esau wept and begged for a blessing after Jacob had received it (Genesis 27:34–38). Many interpreters understand Hebrews to mean that he could not undo what was done: the birthright he had despised was gone, though his tears were real. Hebrews does not teach that God refuses a sinner who truly repents; the whole letter invites the readers to come near the throne of grace (4:16). It warns against trading a lasting gift for a passing appetite.
study: What hardship in my life might God be using to train me? Can I ask for the “peaceful fruit” it may bring?
When I pray, do I compare myself with others? Can I pray the tax collector's prayer slowly today?
